DeutschMagyar

Relationships

Silence can scream, too

In some families, the loudest thing is not the argument. It is what no one feels safe enough to say.

621 SOBER · approximately 6 min read

“My mother’s silence frightened me more than any shouting.”

This essay explores silence and emotional distance in families affected by alcohol. Every family’s situation is different.

Our home was not always loud. That is one reason it took me so long to understand the damage.

There were arguments, but there were also long stretches of careful quiet. Doors closed gently. Questions stayed unfinished. My mother could communicate an entire weather system by the way she placed a cup on the table.

As a child, I learned to read that silence. I watched faces before I spoke. I checked whether the room felt safe. I tried to become easy, useful, and invisible.

No one had to tell me there were subjects we did not touch.

What silence does inside a family

Silence can prevent an argument tonight. It can help a child get through dinner. It can protect someone from retaliation when speaking honestly is not safe. In that sense, silence may be an intelligent survival strategy.

But when silence becomes the permanent rule, reality starts to blur. Family members stop checking their perceptions with one another. Each person carries a private version of the problem. Shame grows in the space where language should be.

Children often assume the tension is their fault. Partners may begin to doubt their own memory. The person drinking can point to the absence of open conflict as proof that nothing is seriously wrong.

The family looks peaceful from outside while everyone inside is listening for the next change in the air.

Speaking does not have to mean confrontation

Breaking silence does not require a dramatic family meeting. It may begin with one honest sentence to a trusted person: “Alcohol is affecting our home, and I am not doing well.”

It may mean writing down what happened before discussing it. Facts are grounding: what you observed, when it happened, and how it affected you. This can help separate direct experience from arguments about motives and labels.

Sometimes the safest first conversation is with a counselor, support group, doctor, or friend rather than with the person drinking. If you fear anger, violence, financial retaliation, or being trapped, safety planning comes before openness.

A new kind of quiet

In recovery, I had to learn that quiet is not always peace and noise is not always danger. An honest disagreement can be healthier than a house organized around avoidance. A pause can be caring when people know the conversation will continue.

You do not need perfect words. You need one place where your experience can be spoken without being minimized. Silence helped many of us survive. It does not have to be where we live forever.

Silence can be protection

People go quiet for many reasons: fear, exhaustion, shame, or the belief that speaking will only make things worse.
